catalog_quote: Stress is not phonemically contrastive in Sare and is partially predictable in that stress rules depend on a division of the word into syllables. For the purposes of stress assignment, the number of syllables corresponds to the number of vowels, with the exception that diphthongs consisting of non-high vowels followed by high vowels (ai, ei, ou) counting as single syllables. In all the words examined, despite their length or number of syllables, the secondary stress (marked as ̀) always falls on the first syllable. new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-contrastive, length-dependent stress: primary stress is word-final in disyllabic roots (tòxú 'head', nàná 'earthquake') and penultimate in roots of three or more syllables (sògánɨ 'call', kàdibóxu 'chair', kàsarédsai 'to lie'); syllable count = vowel count except that ai, ei, ou count as one syllable. A secondary stress always sits on the first syllable. Stress is assigned on the root and stays there when affixes or compound members are added (àmára -> àmára-bogɨ, ɸòxú -> ɸòxú-ogu), so in inflected words primary stress need not be penultimate/final of the whole word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress 'always falls on the first syllable' of the word regardless of length (tì, tògai, kɨ̀meyiaru, tàitsambra).
new_statements.exceptions: Disyllables take final rather than penultimate primary stress; affixed and compounded forms keep the root's stress position rather than recomputing over the longer word. No lexical exceptions listed; author says the pattern held 'in all the words examined'.
new_statements.domain_note: Rule stated over the root/citation form; explicitly says suffixed and compounded words retain root stress, so the domain of the final/penult computation is the root, not the phonological word. Two dialects (Blackwater, Korosmeri) not distinguished for stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Sumbuk calls the language Sare and states (p. 1) it is 'also known in the literature as Wasare or Kapriman', spoken by the Kapriman people on the Blackwater and Korosmeri rivers = Glottolog kapr1245 / ISO dju. He distinguishes two dialects, Blackwater (B, the more widely spoken, author's own) and Korosmeri (K, Mugumute village), >96% cognate; the stress description is given for the language as a whole without dialect qualification.

sources.note: Ch.2 sec. 2.2.1 'Stress' (pp. 40-42): stress not phonemically contrastive; secondary stress always on the first syllable; primary stress on the last syllable of disyllables and on the penultimate syllable of words of three or more syllables (ai, ei, ou count as one syllable); affixed and compounded forms keep stress on the root. Marked examples: tòxú 'head', sògánɨ 'call', kàdibóxu 'chair', àmára-bogɨ 'parcel of fish'.
